# selectbench

**selectbench runs several variable selection methods on the same data, shows
which variables each one picks, and scores the methods against the truth on
simulated data.**

## The problem it solves

Suppose you have an outcome and ten possible predictors, and you want to know
which predictors to keep in the model. Variable selection methods answer this
question automatically, but different methods give different answers on the
same data. Choosing one method and reporting its answer hides that.

selectbench puts the answers side by side. The data below are simulated so
that only `x1`, `x2` and `x3` affect the outcome `y`. The other seven
variables are noise.

```{r}
library(selectbench)

result <- compare_selection(y ~ ., data = selection_demo, seed = 1)
result
```

Every method found `x1`, `x2` and `x3`. Four of the six also picked up noise
variables: forward AIC, backward AIC and the lasso at its smallest penalty
picked three each, and the lasso at one standard error picked one. Only the
two BIC based methods found exactly the true variables. The same table as a
plot, with the true variables marked by a star:

```{r compare-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.8, fig.alt = "Tile plot with ten variables in rows and six selection methods in columns. All methods select x1, x2 and x3. Three methods also select x6, x9 and x10, and one selects x6 only."}
plot(result, truth = c("x1", "x2", "x3"))
```

When you use your own data you will not know the truth. What you can see is
which variables every method agrees on and which ones depend on the method
chosen. When you do know the truth, as in a simulation, `score_selection()`
and `simulate_selection()` tell you which method does best.

## Functions

| Function | What it does |
|----------|--------------|
| `compare_selection()` | Runs the selection methods on your data and returns a table of which variable each method selected |
| `plot()` on its result | Draws that table, with the most widely selected variables at the top |
| `simulate_selection_data()` | Generates data in which you choose the true variables |
| `score_selection()` | For one comparison with a known truth, counts the true variables found and the noise variables picked |
| `simulate_selection()` | Repeats the whole experiment over many simulated data sets and averages the scores |
| `plot()` on its result | Plots every method by how many true variables it finds and how many noise variables it picks |

## Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("Jimmuji/selectbench")
```

Then load it:

```{r}
library(selectbench)
```

## How to use it

### 1. Compare methods on your data

Give `compare_selection()` a formula and a data frame, the same way you would
for `lm()`.

```{r}
compare_selection(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars, seed = 1)
```

Rows with a missing value in any variable that is used are dropped first, so
that every method sees the same data. The `seed` makes the result the same
every time. It matters for the lasso, which chooses its penalty by randomly
splitting the data.

For a yes or no outcome, use `family = "binomial"`. The outcome can be 0 and 1,
`TRUE` and `FALSE`, or a factor with two levels.

### 2. Choose the methods

```{r}
compare_selection(y ~ ., data = selection_demo,
                  methods = c("both_aic", "both_bic", "lasso_1se"), seed = 1)$table
```

| Method | What it does |
|--------|--------------|
| `forward_aic`, `forward_bic` | Forward stepwise. Starts with no predictors and adds the one that improves the criterion most, until nothing improves it |
| `backward_aic`, `backward_bic` | Backward stepwise. Starts with all predictors and removes the least useful one at a time |
| `both_aic`, `both_bic` | Stepwise in both directions. Starts with no predictors, and can also remove a variable it added earlier |
| `lasso_min` | The lasso, with the penalty that gives the smallest error in cross-validation. A variable is selected if its coefficient is not zero |
| `lasso_1se` | The lasso, with the largest penalty whose error is within one standard error of the smallest. Selects fewer variables |
| `best_aic`, `best_bic` | Best subset. Checks every combination of variables and picks the best one by AIC or BIC. Linear models only, up to 25 predictor columns |

AIC and BIC both reward a model that fits well and penalise one that has many
variables. BIC penalises more, so it keeps fewer variables.

A categorical variable with several levels is turned into several columns. It
counts as selected if any of its columns is, so each row of the table is one
variable from your formula.

### 3. Score the methods when you know the truth

Use `simulate_selection_data()` to make data in which you decide which
variables matter. The first `length(beta)` variables have the effects in
`beta`, and the rest are noise.

```{r}
set.seed(10)
d <- simulate_selection_data(n = 100, p = 10, beta = c(1, -0.8, 0.6), rho = 0.5)
attr(d, "truth")

one <- compare_selection(y ~ ., d, seed = 1)
score_selection(one, truth = attr(d, "truth"))
```

`sensitivity` is the share of true variables that were found.
`false_positive_rate` is the share of noise variables that were picked.
`exact` is `TRUE` when the method picked the true variables and nothing else.

### 4. Repeat it many times

One data set can favour a method by luck. `simulate_selection()` repeats the
experiment on many simulated data sets and averages the scores. The example
below uses weak effects, a sample of 100 and correlated predictors, which is
a hard case.

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_selection(
  n = 100, p = 10, beta = c(0.8, -0.6, 0.5), rho = 0.5,
  methods = c("forward_aic", "backward_aic", "both_aic", "forward_bic",
              "backward_bic", "both_bic", "lasso_min", "lasso_1se",
              "best_aic", "best_bic"),
  n_sim = 500, seed = 2025
)
sim
```

`exact` is the share of the 500 data sets in which the method found exactly the
three true variables. `mcse_exact` is the Monte Carlo standard error of that
share, which says how much of the difference between two methods could be
chance.

```{r sim-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Scatter plot of ten selection methods. The BIC stepwise methods and best subset BIC sit near the top left with few false positives. The AIC methods are further right. The lasso at its smallest penalty is far to the right, and the lasso at one standard error is lower and to the left."}
plot(sim)
```

A method in the top left corner finds the true variables without picking up
noise. In this setting the BIC methods and best subset with BIC have the
fewest noise variables, the AIC methods find slightly more true variables at
the cost of more noise, and the lasso at its smallest penalty picks up the
most noise.

Every data set is generated with the seed `seed + i`, so the result is the
same each time and does not depend on the number of cores used.

## Limits

* Best subset is only available for linear models, and for at most 25 predictor
  columns.
* Only main effects are supported, not interactions.
* The outcome must be a single column.

## How it differs from other packages

[`StepReg`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=StepReg) runs several stepwise
strategies and criteria in one call, and
[`featR`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=featR) puts many feature selection
methods behind one interface. Neither one lays out the selections of different
methods in one comparison table or plot, and neither scores the methods against
a known truth. selectbench does both, and repeats the scoring over simulated data
sets.

## Getting help

Every function and the example data have a help page with examples:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?compare_selection
?simulate_selection
help(package = "selectbench")
```
